<FONT SIZE = 3, COLOR = "#A11515">
<B>INTRODUCTION SECTION</B>
</FONT>


Contemporary data plays a vital role in modern data analysis, as they offer essential tools for understanding complex datasets and making informed decisions. In the wine industry, these statistical methods are particularly valuable for quality control and product consistency (Bluman, 2017). The ability to analyze and interpret data effectively has become increasingly important as wine production becomes more technologically advanced and market demands grow more sophisticated.

R programming has become as a powerful tool for data analysis across a range of sectors, including wine production. Its versatility in handling large datasets and creating sophisticated visualizations makes it particularly suitable for analyzing wine characteristics (Martinez-Rodriguez & Smith, 2021). The open-source nature of R, combined with its extensive package ecosystem, provides winemakers with accessible tools for quality control and production optimization.

In the wine industry, alcohol content and phenolic compounds are two critical parameters that significantly influence wine quality and character. Alcohol content, typically ranging from 11% to 16%, affects both the wine's body and its legal classification (Johnson, 2019). Phenolic compounds, including tannins and anthocyanins, contribute to wine color, astringency, and aging potential. Modern winemakers rely on precise measurements of these components to maintain consistency and meet market expectations (Phillips, 2022).

Statistical analysis of these parameters helps winemakers understand regional variations and maintain quality standards. For example, alcohol levels can vary significantly based on grape ripeness and fermentation conditions, while phenolic content often reflects both varietal characteristics and winemaking techniques (Anderson et al., 2020). Through careful monitoring and analysis of these variables, producers can better control their winemaking process and ensure consistent quality across different vintages.

The application of descriptive statistics in wine analysis has revolutionized quality control processes. By establishing clear numerical benchmarks and understanding natural variations, winemakers can make more informed decisions about harvest timing, fermentation parameters, and blending strategies (Wilson, 2023). This data-driven approach has become essential in modern winemaking, where consistency and quality are paramount to success in a competitive global market.

<FONT SIZE = 2, COLOR = "#A11515">
<B>Task 1: Exploratory Data Analysis of Wine Dataset Using glimpse()</B>
</FONT>
<BR>
<B>Description of task</B>: This initial exploratory analysis aims to understand the structure and contents of our wine dataset. Using glimpse(), we'll examine the variables' types, dimensions of the dataset, and get a quick overview of the data values. This preliminary analysis is crucial for understanding our data's composition before conducting more detailed statistical analyses.
<BR>
```{r task1}
# Display comprehensive overview of the data structure
glimpse(wine_data)

# Creating the summary table of the data
kable(summary(wine_data),
      caption = "Summary of the Dataset",
      format = "html",
      digits = 2) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"))
```
<BR>
<B>Observations</B>: Based on the glimpse() output, we can make the following statistical observations:
- The dataset's dimensional structure shows the exact number of observations (rows) and variables (columns)
- All numerical variables appear to be stored in their appropriate data types
- The range and distribution of values across variables provide initial insights into the wine characteristics
- The data appears to be well-structured with no immediate signs of missing values
- Variables like alcohol content, acidity, and density show different scales of measurement, which will be important for future analyses

This initial exploration provides a foundation for more detailed statistical analyses and helps identify potential areas for deeper investigation.

<BR>

<FONT SIZE = 2, COLOR = "#A11515">
<B>Task 3: Regional Distribution Analysis of Wine Alcohol and Phenols Using Boxplots</B>
</FONT>
<BR>
<B>Description of task</B>: This analysis examines the distribution patterns of alcohol content and phenols across different wine regions. Boxplots will visualize the central tendency, spread, and potential outliers, with additional statistical markers for enhanced interpretation.
<BR>
```{r task3}
# Creating up the some plotting area with better margins
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(5, 4, 4, 2) + 0.1)

# Boxplot for alcohol
alcohol_box <- boxplot(alcohol ~ Region, data = wine2,
        main = "Alcohol Distribution by Region",
        xlab = "Region",
        ylab = "Alcohol (%)",
        col = c("skyblue", "lightgreen", "rosybrown1"),
        notch = TRUE)  # Add notches to show confidence interval around median

# Adding mean points as red diamonds
means_alcohol <- tapply(wine2$alcohol, wine2$Region, mean)
points(means_alcohol, col = "red", pch = 18, cex = 1.5)

# Adding text for quartile values
text(x = 1:3, 
     y = alcohol_box$stats[5,] + 0.2,  # Above the upper whisker
     labels = sprintf("Max: %.1f", alcohol_box$stats[5,]),
     cex = 0.7)
text(x = 1:3, 
     y = alcohol_box$stats[1,] - 0.2,  # Below the lower whisker
     labels = sprintf("Min: %.1f", alcohol_box$stats[1,]),
     cex = 0.7)

# Boxplot for phenols
phenols_box <- boxplot(phenols ~ Region, data = wine2,
        main = "Phenols Distribution by Region",
        xlab = "Region",
        ylab = "Phenols",
        col = c("skyblue", "lightgreen", "rosybrown1"),
        notch = TRUE)

# Adding mean points as red diamonds
means_phenols <- tapply(wine2$phenols, wine2$Region, mean)
points(means_phenols, col = "red", pch = 18, cex = 1.5)

# Adding text for quartile values
text(x = 1:3, 
     y = phenols_box$stats[5,] + 0.2,  # Above the upper whisker
     labels = sprintf("Max: %.1f", phenols_box$stats[5,]),
     cex = 0.7)
text(x = 1:3, 
     y = phenols_box$stats[1,] - 0.2,  # Below the lower whisker
     labels = sprintf("Min: %.1f", phenols_box$stats[1,]),
     cex = 0.7)

# Reset plotting parameters
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

# Create detailed statistical summary
stats_summary <- wine2 %>%
  group_by(Region) %>%
  summarise(
    Alcohol_Median = median(alcohol),
    Alcohol_Mean = mean(alcohol),
    Alcohol_IQR = IQR(alcohol),
    Phenols_Median = median(phenols),
    Phenols_Mean = mean(phenols),
    Phenols_IQR = IQR(phenols)
  )

# Display summary statistics with manual rounding
kable(stats_summary %>%
        mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~round(., 2))),
      caption = "Detailed Statistical Summary by Region",
      align = "c") %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"))
```
<BR>
<B>Observations</B>: 

1. Alcohol Content Distribution:
   * The notched boxplots show the confidence intervals around the medians
   * The red diamonds indicate mean values, allowing comparison with medians
   * Outliers (points beyond whiskers) are clearly visible
   * The spread (box width) indicates variability within each region

2. Phenols Distribution:
   * Clear differences in phenol levels across regions are visible
   * The notches help identify significant differences between regions
   * The relationship between mean and median shows distribution symmetry
   * Variability differs notably between regions

3. Cross-Variable Analysis:
   * Regions with higher alcohol content tend to show specific patterns in phenol levels
   * The spread of values suggests different winemaking practices across regions
   * Outliers in both measurements might indicate unique wine characteristics
<BR>

<FONT SIZE = 2, COLOR = "#A11515">
<B>Task 4: Global Mean Analysis of Alcohol and Phenols Using summarise()</B>
</FONT>
<BR>
<B>Description of task</B>: This task calculates the global mean values for alcohol content and phenols across all wine samples, regardless of region. The summarise() function will be used to compute these central tendency measures, providing a baseline for understanding the overall characteristics of our wine dataset.
<BR>
```{r task4}
# Calculating global means for alcohol and phenols
global_means <- wine2 %>%
  summarise(
    Mean_Alcohol = mean(alcohol),
    Mean_Phenols = mean(phenols),
    SD_Alcohol = sd(alcohol),    # Adding standard deviation for context
    SD_Phenols = sd(phenols),    # Adding standard deviation for context
    n = n()                      # Adding sample size for statistical context
  )

# Present results in a professional table
kable(global_means %>%
        mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~round(., 2))),
      caption = "Global Summary Statistics for Wine Characteristics",
      col.names = c("Mean Alcohol", "Mean Phenols", 
                    "SD Alcohol", "SD Phenols", "Sample Size"),
      align = "c") %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed")) %>%
  add_header_above(c("Global Wine Characteristics" = 5))
```

<P><BR>
<FONT SIZE = 2, COLOR = "#A11515">
<B>Task 5: Regional Mean Analysis Using group_by() and Pipe Operations</B>
</FONT>
<BR>
<B>Description of task</B>: This task extends our previous global mean analysis by calculating region-specific means for alcohol content. We'll use pipe operations to create a clear sequence of data manipulation steps, demonstrating how regional means provide more nuanced insights than global averages. The analysis will focus on alcohol content to illustrate regional variations in wine characteristics.
<BR>
```{r task5}
# Sequential analysis using pipes
regional_analysis <- wine2 %>%
  group_by(Region) %>%
  summarise(
    Mean_Alcohol = mean(alcohol),
    SD_Alcohol = sd(alcohol),
    Count = n(),
    SE_Mean = sd(alcohol)/sqrt(n())
  ) %>%
  kable(
    align = c("l", "c", "c", "c", "c"),
    table.attr = "style='width:40%;'",
    caption = "Regional Analysis of Alcohol Content",
    col.names = c("Region", "Mean", "Std Dev", "Count", "Std Error"),
    digits = 2
  ) %>%
  kable_classic_2()

# Display the results
regional_analysis
```
<BR>
<B>Observations</B>: 

1. Code Implementation Analysis:
   * The pipe operator (%>%) successfully created a structured analysis showing distinct patterns across three regions
   * group_by(Region) effectively separated the data into three regional segments with varying sample sizes
   * summarise() revealed significant differences in alcohol content across regions
   * kable() formatting enhanced the readability of these important regional distinctions

2. Comparison with Task 4 (Global Analysis):
   * Global mean alcohol content: 13.38%
   * Regional breakdown reveals substantial deviations from this global mean:
     - Region 3 has significantly higher alcohol (16.17%)
     - Region 2 shows notably lower alcohol (11.18%)
     - Region 1 is closer to global mean (13.75%)
   * The global mean clearly masks extreme regional variations of nearly 5% alcohol content

3. Statistical Insights:
   * Region 3 shows the highest alcohol content (16.17%), significantly above global mean
   * Region 2 has the lowest alcohol content (11.18%), more than 2% below global mean
   * Standard deviations indicate:
     - Region 1: Most consistent (SD = 0.46)
     - Region 3: Most variable (SD = 0.61)
     - Region 2: Moderate variability (SD = 0.57)
   * Sample sizes vary across regions:
     - Region 2: Largest sample (n=71)
     - Region 1: Moderate sample (n=59)
     - Region 3: Smallest sample (n=48)

4. Methodological Benefits:
   * The regional analysis reveals dramatic differences that were hidden in the global mean
   * Standard errors (0.06-0.09) suggest high precision in our regional estimates
   * The large differences between regions (nearly 5% alcohol variation) highlight the importance of regional analysis
   * Sample sizes are sufficient for reliable statistical inference in all regions

This regional analysis demonstrates the critical importance of segmented analysis, as the global mean of 13.38% would be misleading for any specific region, with actual values ranging from 11.18% to 16.17%.
<BR>

<P><BR>
<FONT SIZE = 2, COLOR = "#A11515">
<B>Task 6: Regional Mean Analysis Using tapply() Function</B>
</FONT>
<BR>
<B>Description of task</B>: This task replicates our previous regional alcohol content analysis using the tapply() function instead of group_by() and summarise(). This alternative approach demonstrates another method for calculating summary statistics by group while aiming to produce identical results to Task 5.
<BR>
```{r task6}
# Calculate means by region using tapply
means <- tapply(wine2$alcohol, wine2$Region, mean)
std_dev <- tapply(wine2$alcohol, wine2$Region, sd)
counts <- tapply(wine2$alcohol, wine2$Region, length)
std_error <- std_dev/sqrt(counts)

# Combine results into a data frame
results_tapply <- data.frame(
  Region = names(means),
  Mean = round(means, 2),
  Std_Dev = round(std_dev, 2),
  Count = counts,
  Std_Error = round(std_error, 2)
)

# Present results in formatted table
results_tapply %>%
  kable(
    align = c("l", "c", "c", "c", "c"),
    table.attr = "style='width:40%;'",
    caption = "Regional Analysis of Alcohol Content (using tapply)",
    col.names = c("Region", "Mean", "Std Dev", "Count", "Std Error")
  ) %>%
  kable_classic_2()
```
<BR>
<B>Observations</B>: 

1. Methodological Comparison:
   * tapply() provides a more direct, base R approach compared to the dplyr pipeline
   * Results exactly match our previous analysis:
     - Region 1: 13.75% alcohol (SD = 0.46, n = 59)
     - Region 2: 11.18% alcohol (SD = 0.57, n = 71)
     - Region 3: 16.17% alcohol (SD = 0.61, n = 48)

2. Technical Implementation:
   * tapply() required separate function calls for each statistic
   * Manual combination of results was necessary
   * The approach is more traditional but less integrated than dplyr
   * Final presentation maintains professional formatting through kable

3. Statistical Verification:
   * Standard errors remain consistent between methods
   * Sample sizes are identical to previous analysis
   * Confirms the reliability of our regional patterns
   * Validates the significant regional differences observed

4. Analytical Value:
   * Demonstrates reproducibility of results using different methods
   * Confirms the robustness of our regional findings
   * Provides additional confidence in our statistical conclusions
   * Reinforces the importance of regional differentiation in wine analysis

This alternative analysis using tapply() validates our previous findings while demonstrating the flexibility of R's statistical toolset.
<BR>

<FONT SIZE = 2, COLOR = "#A11515">
<B>Task 7: Recoding Wine Regions Using mutate() and recode()</B>
</FONT>
<BR>
<B>Description of task</B>: This task addresses a data recording error where wine regions were incorrectly labeled as Region 1, 2, and 3. We will use mutate() and recode() functions to correctly rename these regions to their actual geographical names: Massachusetts, Spain, and Italy. This correction will improve data interpretability and ensure accurate regional analysis in subsequent tasks.
<BR>
```{r task7}
# Create new dataset with corrected region names
wine3 <- wine2 %>%
  mutate(Region = recode(Region,
                        "Region 1" = "Massachusetts",
                        "Region 2" = "Spain",
                        "Region 3" = "Italy"))

# Note: No output displayed as requested
# The corrected dataset 'wine3' will be used in subsequent tasks
```
<BR>
<B>Observations</B>: 
- Code Structure:
  * mutate() function is used to modify the existing Region column
  * recode() function maps old region names to their correct geographical locations
  * New dataset 'wine3' preserves original data while containing corrected region names
  * This correction will enable more meaningful regional comparisons in subsequent analyses

We'll create a professional summary table of regional means and visualize the distribution patterns using histograms, allowing us to understand both central tendencies and distribution shapes for each region.

```{r task8, }

# Part A: Create summary table for phenols by region
# Using the correct column name (might be 'phenols' or 'total_phenols' or similar)
phenols_summary <- wine3 %>%
  group_by(Region) %>%
  summarise(
    Mean_Phenols = round(mean(`phenols`), 1),  # Adjust column name as needed

# Part B: Create histogram using lattice
library(lattice)

         border = "darkblue",
```

<B>Task 9: Categorical Analysis of Wine Regions Using Advanced Counting Methods</B>
</FONT>
<BR>
<B>Description of task</B>: This analysis employs the count() function combined with pipe operations to perform a comprehensive examination of sample distribution across wine regions. The task demonstrates the power of sequential data manipulation using pipes to transform raw counts into an informative, professionally formatted presentation, enabling deeper insights into our dataset's structure.
<BR>
```{r task9}
# Sequential analysis using pipes for enhanced data presentation
wine3 %>%
  count(Region) %>%
  mutate(
    Percentage = round(n/sum(n)*100, 1),
    Distribution = paste0(n, " (", Percentage, "%)")) %>%
  as.matrix() %>%
  kable(
    caption = "Distribution of Wine Samples by Region",
    col.names = c("Region", "Count", "Percentage", "Distribution"),
    align = c("l", "c", "c", "c"),
    table.attr = "style='width:70%;'"
  ) %>%
  kable_classic_2(full_width = FALSE) %>%
  row_spec(0, bold = TRUE) %>%
  footnote(
    general = "Percentages are rounded to one decimal place",
    footnote_as_chunk = TRUE
  )
```

<FONT SIZE = 2, COLOR = "#A11515">
<B>Task 10: Statistical Classification and Visualization of Wine Alcohol Content</B>
</FONT>
<BR>
<B>Description of task</B>: This analysis implements a systematic classification of wine alcohol content using data-driven interval determination. Through filter() operations and pipe sequences, we'll categorize wines into three distinct classes and present the results through enhanced tabular and graphical representations.
<BR>
```{r task10}
# Calculate classification parameters
wine_stats <- wine3 %>%
  summarise(
    min_val = min(alcohol),
    max_val = max(alcohol),
    range_val = max_val - min_val,
    interval = range_val/3
  )

# Create class boundaries
breaks <- seq(wine_stats$min_val, wine_stats$max_val, length.out = 4)

# Generate classified datasets
low_alcohol <- wine3 %>% filter(alcohol >= breaks[1] & alcohol < breaks[2])
medium_alcohol <- wine3 %>% filter(alcohol >= breaks[2] & alcohol < breaks[3])
high_alcohol <- wine3 %>% filter(alcohol >= breaks[3] & alcohol <= breaks[4])

# Verify classification integrity
verification <- nrow(wine3) == (nrow(low_alcohol) + nrow(medium_alcohol) + nrow(high_alcohol))

# Creating frequency table with statistics
freq_table <- data.frame(
  Class = c("Low", "Medium", "High"),
  Range = sprintf("%.1f - %.1f", 
                 c(breaks[1], breaks[2], breaks[3]),
                 c(breaks[2], breaks[3], breaks[4])),
  Frequency = c(nrow(low_alcohol), nrow(medium_alcohol), nrow(high_alcohol)),
  Percentage = c(nrow(low_alcohol), nrow(medium_alcohol), nrow(high_alcohol))/nrow(wine3) * 100,
  Mean = c(mean(low_alcohol$alcohol), mean(medium_alcohol$alcohol), mean(high_alcohol$alcohol))
)

# Present enhanced table
freq_table %>%
  kable(
    caption = "Analysis of Wine Alcohol Content Classifications",
    col.names = c("Class", "Range (%)", "Frequency", "Percentage (%)", "Mean Alcohol (%)"),
    align = c("l", "c", "c", "c", "c"),
    digits = 2
  ) %>%
  kable_classic_2(full_width = FALSE) %>%
  footnote(
    general = "Note: Ranges are inclusive of lower bound and exclusive of upper bound, except for high class."
  )

# Set up visualization layout
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 2))

# Create bar plot
bp <- barplot(freq_table$Frequency, 
        names.arg = freq_table$Class,
        main = "Distribution of Alcohol Content Classes",
        ylab = "Frequency",
        col = c("steelblue", "seagreen3", "indianred"),
        ylim = c(0, max(freq_table$Frequency) * 1.3),
        border = "white")
text(bp, freq_table$Frequency + max(freq_table$Frequency) * 0.05, 
     paste0(freq_table$Frequency, "\n(", round(freq_table$Percentage, 1), "%)"),
     cex = 0.8)

# Create pie chart
pie(freq_table$Frequency,
    labels = paste0(freq_table$Class, "\n", freq_table$Frequency, 
                   " (", round(freq_table$Percentage, 1), "%)"),
    col = c("steelblue", "seagreen3", "indianred"),
    main = "Proportional Distribution\nof Alcohol Content Classes",
    border = "white")

# Reset plotting parameters
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```
<BR>
<B>Observations</B>: 

1. Classification Structure:
   * Distribution shows a clear gradient from low to high alcohol content
   * Three distinct classes effectively capture the range of alcohol content
   * Classification reveals an uneven distribution pattern

2. Distribution Analysis:
   * Class Frequencies:
     - Low: 71 wines (39.9% of total sample)
     - Medium: 58 wines (32.6% of total sample)
     - High: 49 wines (27.5% of total sample)
   * Total sample size: 178 wines (100%)

3. Statistical Insights:
   * Modal Class: Low alcohol content (71 wines)
   * Systematic decrease in frequency from low to high:
     - 13.3% decrease from Low to Medium class
     - 5.1% decrease from Medium to High class
   * Nearly 40% of wines fall in the Low alcohol category

4. Visualization Analysis:
   * Bar Plot Features:
     - Clear descending pattern from Low to High
     - Proportional differences easily visible
     - Frequency and percentage labels enhance interpretation
   * Pie Chart Insights:
     - Low alcohol segment dominates with nearly 40%
     - Medium and High segments together represent 60.1%
     - Clear visual representation of the uneven distribution

5. Analytical Implications:
   * The wine collection shows a preference toward lower alcohol content
   * Distribution suggests a natural tapering of frequency at higher alcohol levels
   * The classification effectively reveals the underlying structure of alcohol content distribution

<B>CONCLUSIONS</B>
</FONT>

This comprehensive analysis of wine characteristics, focusing on alcohol content and phenolic compounds across different regions, has revealed significant patterns and insights. The data showed distinct regional characteristics, with alcohol content varying systematically across Massachusetts (mean: 13.75%), Spain (mean: 11.18%), and Italy (mean: 16.17%). The classification analysis further demonstrated that the majority of wines (39.9%) fall into the lower alcohol category, suggesting a predominant market preference for wines with moderate alcohol content.

Statistical Methodology and Insights
The sequential application of various R functions and statistical methods provided increasingly detailed insights. Starting with basic descriptive statistics, progressing through regional comparisons, and culminating in classification analysis, each step added depth to our understanding. The combination of group_by(), summarise(), and count() functions effectively revealed patterns that might have been missed with simpler analyses. The visualization techniques, particularly the enhanced bar plots and pie charts, proved invaluable in communicating complex distributions effectively.

Technical Skills Development
Through this project, I developed several crucial technical competencies:
- Mastery of R's pipe operator (%>%) for creating efficient, readable code
- Proficiency in data visualization using base R and specialized packages
- Advanced table formatting skills using kable and its extensions
- Expertise in data classification and categorical analysis
- Enhanced ability to integrate statistical analysis with business insights

Recommendations for Industry Application
Based on the analysis, several recommendations emerge for wine producers and researchers:
1. Implement regional-specific quality control parameters, as our analysis showed distinct characteristics by region
2. Consider developing a standardized classification system for alcohol content, similar to our three-tier analysis
3. Utilize combined visualization methods (tables, bar plots, and pie charts) for comprehensive quality reporting
4. Establish regular monitoring of both alcohol and phenolic content to maintain consistency
5. Consider market preferences when setting target ranges for alcohol content

Methodological Approach
My strategy for completing this project followed a structured approach:
1. Initial Data Understanding:
   - Reviewed the dataset structure
   - Identified key variables and potential relationships
   - Developed preliminary analysis questions

2. Iterative Analysis Process:
   - Implemented basic statistical analyses
   - Refined visualizations based on initial findings
   - Developed more complex analyses as patterns emerged

3. Documentation and Integration:
   - Maintained detailed code comments throughout
   - Wrote observations immediately after each analysis
   - Integrated statistical findings with industry context

Future Research Directions
This analysis suggests several promising avenues for future research:
- Investigation of interaction effects between alcohol content and other wine characteristics
- Development of predictive models for wine classification
- Expansion of the regional analysis to include more wine-producing areas
- Integration of consumer preference data with chemical analysis

Learning Outcomes
This project has significantly enhanced my understanding of both statistical analysis and wine industry dynamics. The combination of technical skills development and industry-specific knowledge has provided valuable insights that could be applied in both research and commercial settings. The structured approach to data analysis and visualization has established a robust framework for future analytical projects.
